video_title: One Step Away From Sell | WAYT?
gist: This is an episode of What Are Your Thoughts? with Josh Brown and Michael Batnick, not Animal Spirits with Ben Carlson, despite the channel label. They argue over whether BofA's Sell Side Indicator, now 30bp from a sell signal, matters while the index sits at all-time highs: Batnick says the market is 'daring you to sell', and Brown expects an October VIX spike given a flatlining VIX, 5.3% 10-year yields and breadth breaking down. Standout segments cover FICO's mortgage-scoring monopoly vanishing in summer 2026 as VantageScore went from 0% to 41% at Rocket, Burry's GPU-depreciation bear case falling apart, and refiners (Valero, Phillips, Marathon) posting AI-like returns.

themes.theme: Sentiment: no fear, lots of doubt

insights.claim: Bank of America's Sell Side Indicator, which tracks sell-side strategists' average recommended equity allocation in a balanced fund and is read as a contrarian signal, rose in September and is now just 30 basis points from a sell signal.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A sell trigger on a widely followed contrarian gauge could arrive within weeks and give bears a headline, though the hosts warn it is not a precise timing tool.
insights.quote: sellside indicator increased in September and is now just 30 basis points from a sell signal

insights.claim: BofA also notes that the AAII bull-bear spread fell to about minus 25 percentage points in mid-September, roughly 1.5 standard deviations away from its 10-year average, and that S&P 500 forward 12-month returns have historically been slightly stronger when that spread was well below its average. The signal is noisy, which offsets the strategist-bullishness warning.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown (quoting Savita Subramanian)
insights.so_what: Strategists are bullish but retail survey respondents are still bearish, so the sentiment picture is mixed rather than euphoric.

insights.claim: 2026 sums up as 'no fear, tons of doubt': the VIX sits around 16, while doubt shows up as falling multiples even as companies post record earnings above consensus and raise guidance, with the market up 14% on the year and earnings up much more.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown (expanding on Michael Batnick's comment)
insights.so_what: Prices are trailing earnings, so P/E compression is leaving room for further upside if doubt fades rather than signaling a top.
insights.quote: I would say no fear, tons of doubt

insights.claim: Strategist allocations and the low VIX are being held up partly by career risk: allocators are 'tired of being rugpulled', and every time they cut equity exposure or S&P targets they look wrong a month later, so nobody wants to turn bearish.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Bullish strategist positioning may reflect fear of looking wrong more than conviction. That makes the SSI a weaker contrarian signal, but it could also mean a fast reversal if they all capitulate at once.
insights.quote: These guys do not want to get bearish. They don't want to get Mike Wilson.

insights.claim: Over the past 17-18 years the market's message has been 'I dare you to sell', and the index is not even in a 5% pullback from its high despite many visible risks.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Resilience through bad news argues for staying long rather than front-running a sell signal.
insights.quote: the message of the market is I dare you to sell

insights.claim: Equity ETF inflows have cooled dramatically, a hard flow data point that runs against the idea of extreme bullishness.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Slowing flows suggest positioning is not frothy. Watch for flows to re-accelerate as a sign of late-cycle euphoria.
insights.quote: equity ETF inflows have cooled dramatically. That is not a feeling. That is a data point.

insights.claim: Nasdaq earnings growth of about 36% explains why investors feel they cannot sell, and because earnings are probably the most important input in strategists' allocation models, their bullishness is understandable.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: As long as earnings keep beating, strategist allocations will stay high. The risk is an earnings disappointment, not the sentiment reading.
insights.quote: 36% earnings growth for the NASDAQ will will do that to you.

insights.claim: Renaissance Macro's Jeff deGraaf flags that the VIX (16.39) has flatlined since March while JPMorgan Global FX volatility and the MOVE bond-volatility index are elevated. Volatility is showing up in currencies and bonds while 'the stock market is in a coma'.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown (citing Jeff deGraaf)
insights.so_what: Equity volatility looks cheap next to cross-asset volatility, so hedging or long-volatility positions may be inexpensive.
insights.quote: you've got volatility in bond yields, got volatility in currencies, the stock market is in a coma

insights.claim: The VIX is being suppressed because the two largest S&P stocks, Apple (in a product cycle) and Nvidia (back-to-back record highs), are at highs, Microsoft has stabilized, Meta is rallying and Amazon is flat. A VIX for the other 493 stocks would look very different.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Headline volatility understates stress in the average stock, so look at single-stock or small-cap volatility indexes instead.
insights.quote: These are the gigantic stocks that are pacifying the VIX

insights.claim: Renaissance Macro's market cycle clock is in the upper-right growth-and-inflation zone it occupied in 2018, a year with two S&P bear-type declines of -17% and -21%, and on October 1, 1987. RenMac says bad things tend to happen there when the Fed is raising rates, though it is not calling for a crash.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown (citing Renaissance Macro)
insights.so_what: Historical analogs point to elevated drawdown risk while the Fed's bias is still to tighten.
insights.quote: bad things tend to happen when growth and inflation are in a similar position with the Fed raising rates

insights.claim: The Fed looks to be on pause through at least October, but per Neil Dutta its bias is to stay tight, and a hike before any cut is the likely sequence.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown (citing Neil Dutta)
insights.so_what: Rate-cut hopes are misplaced, so position for higher-for-longer.
insights.quote: probably a a tightening before a cutting

insights.claim: A material market decline needs something investors don't already know: a 5.3% 10-year yield, inflation and Fed policy are all known. A 6% 10-year yield would probably be enough to trigger one.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Treat 6% on the 10-year as the level that could break equities, and focus on unknown shocks rather than known risks.
insights.quote: 6% on the tenure is what is what pushes everyone over

insights.claim: Candidate surprise shocks include a big-bank miss in the first week of earnings season (Wells Fargo or Bank of America, both in sizable drawdowns, disclosing bond-portfolio problems) or a successful Houthi rocket strike on a pipeline as the Middle East conflict spreads beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Bank earnings in the first week and Middle East energy infrastructure are the tail risks to watch.

insights.claim: Meta and Microsoft talking about pulling back on frontier-model usage could have been a crack in the armor, but the market shrugged it off, a sign that it does not want to sell off right now.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: When the market ignores negative AI-spend headlines, that is a sign of underlying strength.

insights.claim: Brown expects an October surprise and a VIX spike before Thanksgiving. He points to how cheap equity volatility looks against FX and bond volatility, October seasonality, the midterm election and a slow-motion interest-rate shock, and says he would welcome it because he has cash to put to work.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Keep dry powder or hedges ready for a short-term volatility event in October-November.
insights.quote: I think we're going to get a VIC spike this month. I think we're going to get an October surprise.

insights.claim: Brown says he will drop his short-term caution if Q3 financials report a strong consumer, no lending losses and no credit card concerns. He does not expect any downside shock to come from tech earnings.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Bank earnings and their credit commentary are the swing factor for the near-term bear case.

insights.claim: The hosts' wealth firm has clients who are 'egregiously overweight' equities relative to their own plans and is having rebalancing conversations, some of which will lead to trimming.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Advisor-driven rebalancing out of stocks could add selling pressure at the margin.

themes.theme: Bear cases melting: Burry, GPUs, credit

insights.claim: Michael Burry tweeted that the stock market is in the first stage of grief, denial, as in 2000 and 2008, and that this stage lasts six to nine months.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown (reading Michael Burry)
insights.so_what: Burry's call gives bears a timeline, but the hosts see it as one more turn in a long run of bearish calls with shifting goalposts.
insights.quote: in its first stage of grief denial per 2000 and 2008. This stage lasts six to nine months.

insights.claim: Burry's November 2025 bear case, that hyperscalers inflate earnings by extending GPU useful lives, is being undercut: a16z's state-of-markets data shows years-old GPUs holding or gaining rental value amid a continued massive shortage.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Stable used-GPU rental prices weaken the depreciation and accounting bear case on AI capex names.
insights.quote: reports of obsolescence greatly exaggerated

insights.claim: Despite bipartisan political backlash against data centers (moratorium calls, environmental red tape), enough construction is underway and enough states want them that buildout continues. Micron recently raised next-year guidance rather than tempering it.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Political noise around data centers is not stopping capex, so AI suppliers' guidance is credible.
insights.quote: I sort of feel like it's melting like a like an ice sculpture right now

insights.claim: The bear case that investors would stop showing up for AI-related bond auctions can be put to bed: Paramount's debt deal drew about $150 billion of orders, nearly triple the amount sought and one of the largest public bond offerings ever, reflecting how much capital is looking for a home.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Credit markets are wide open for AI and media financing, so a funding squeeze is not a near-term risk.
insights.quote: potential investors placed orders of $150 billion of Paramount debt

insights.claim: The old idea that the bond market is the 'smart money' has been flipped: strong equity prices now drive bond-buyer appetite. Meta's launch of Muse and the stock's roughly 30% rise in two weeks ended worries about Meta's AI data-center bond issuance and separated it from names like CoreWeave.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Equity momentum drives credit spreads for AI issuers, so watch hyperscaler stock prices as the leading signal for their debt.
insights.quote: If the equity is strong, the bond buyers will show up for the bonds. And I think Meta is the best case in point.

insights.claim: As of November 2024, before its current crash, FICO was the best-performing stock since 1990 among the roughly 220 S&P 500 members that were also in the index in 1990. Even after a 60-70% drawdown it ranks about 10th, compounding at about 20% a year.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: The best long-term compounder came from a small monopoly, not a mega-cap, which is a reminder that durable pricing power drives returns.
insights.quote: FICO was the number one performing S&P 500 stock >> since 1990

insights.claim: FICO's sell-off is driven by housing weakness and the software-disruption trade more than by AI-based credit scoring, and above all by regulation: after FICO raised per-score prices sharply (cited as going from 60 cents to as high as $10), FHFA director Bill Pulte opened Fannie and Freddie mortgages to VantageScore.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Aggressive price hikes by a monopoly can invite a regulatory response. Watch other price-hiking monopolies for the same risk.
insights.quote: they got greedy they took their pricing up

insights.claim: VantageScore, owned jointly by TransUnion, Equifax and Experian, went from 0% to 41% of Rocket's mortgage scoring and from 0% to 26% at United starting in May 2026. Rocket says it qualifies more buyers and saves borrowers an average of $1,600 in closing costs per loan.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Share is shifting quickly from FICO to the credit bureaus. That is bearish for FICO's mortgage pricing power and a potential tailwind for TransUnion, Equifax and Experian.
insights.quote: This monopoly was ripped away from Fair Isaac in the span of the summer of 2026.

insights.claim: FICO is the worst-performing S&P 500 stock year to date, down about 60%, even as management raised fiscal 2026 guidance and buys back stock heavily. Analysts at Goldman and Wells Fargo cut it, and securities-fraud investigations are probing whether management misled on regulatory risk.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: This is a rerating of terminal pricing power, like Salesforce's, rather than a fundamental collapse, so a cheap-looking multiple may not mean value.
insights.quote: It's very unusual, very unusual to see a stock down 60% with little fundamental deterioration.

insights.claim: Other companies whose advantage could disappear at the stroke of a pen include Apple, if an antitrust win forces the App Store below its 30% take (catastrophic but slow-moving), and the three dominant refiners, Valero, Phillips 66 and Marathon, since no new US refinery has been built since the 1970s.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Screen holdings for regulatory single points of failure behind monopoly-like margins.

themes.theme: The un-broadening: tech vs everything else

insights.claim: Nvidia is almost $6 trillion, at an all-time high and nearly 9% of the S&P 500, bigger than consumer discretionary or industrials and larger than staples and energy combined.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick (citing Todd Sohn)
insights.so_what: Index concentration means Nvidia alone sets the index's risk.

insights.claim: Nvidia's multiple compression reflects size limits ('scale') and the fact that nearly every active manager must be underweight it, more than doubts about earnings. Even with an expected 85-90% earnings growth quarter, nothing it shows the Street can push the multiple higher.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Do not expect Nvidia's multiple to expand. Returns depend on earnings growth alone.
insights.quote: What can they show the street to push the multiple higher? Nothing.

insights.claim: Nvidia is using its exploding free cash flow to buy back its own stock at around 21 times earnings, so one company's cash flow is supporting its own market cap and helping to hold up the whole market, which Brown calls unprecedented.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Nvidia buybacks act as an index-level backstop, so a slowdown in its cash flow or buybacks would be a systemic risk.
insights.quote: One company's cash flow is enabling it to support its own market cap

insights.claim: Breadth has collapsed. The rolling two-month correlation between S&P tech and the ex-tech market is at its most negative since the bull market began in late 2022. 29% of the Russell 3000 is in a drawdown of 30% or worse since June 1, including about 40% of autos and 47% of software and services stocks. Stocks above their 200-day average fell from 75% to 40%, and only one in three stocks is beating the index, a year-to-date low.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick (citing Duality Research, Negligible Cap, Chart Kid)
insights.so_what: The average stock is in a bear market while the index sits at highs, so stock pickers outside mega-cap tech are getting hurt.
insights.quote: 29% of the Russell 3000 is in a 30% or worse draw down

insights.claim: Duality Research finds that downside breadth divergences, where the other 493 lag mega-cap tech, have not been sell signals in this bull market; the laggards ripped back to catch up. The real warning was when tech weakened while the rest of the market took the baton.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick (citing Duality Research)
insights.so_what: Weak breadth with tech leading is historically benign. Watch for tech to break down while broadening improves.
insights.quote: When the rest of the market has shown strength and the tech sector has shown weakness, that is when you wanted to be cautious

insights.claim: The consumer warning sign Brown takes seriously is weakness in consumer stocks like American Express, Walmart and TJ Maxx, which reach the top and middle of the K-shaped economy. He discounts Home Depot (housing), McDonald's and Pepsi (rate competition) as idiosyncratic.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: AmEx's price action is a read on the affluent consumer. Further weakness there would signal real consumer stress.
insights.quote: To me, American Express is an important stock. >> Uh, and it's it's getting mauled.

themes.theme: Where risk appetite and defense really are

insights.claim: A composite of ARK's seven ETFs is making a technical breakout, which shows money moving out of defensive areas like staples and into speculative risk-on growth, whatever the sentiment surveys say.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Speculative growth leading is a risk-on signal, but it can reverse in an instant.

insights.claim: Brown argues that in 2026 Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia serve as the market's defensive 'easy button'. Staples and utilities are not truly defensive now because they are rate-sensitive: a roughly 3% dividend cannot compete with a 5% Treasury yield, and staples also face high oil prices and a weak low-end consumer. Batnick rejects this, saying the Mag 7 are not defensive.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Classic defensive rotation may not protect portfolios while yields are this high, and mega-cap tech crowding is partly a hiding-place trade.
insights.quote: I think they're buying Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia.

insights.claim: Refiners Valero, Phillips 66 and Marathon are the top three performers in the XLE this year and have broken away from the energy sector. Valero is up about 120% this year, from about $100 a share in late 2024 to over $400, with diesel the key driver rather than oil or natural gas.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Diesel cracks and limited refining capacity are a sector-independent driver. Momentum is strong, but the run is mature.
insights.quote: there is a lot of diesel and diesel is is a big part of the positive story for the refiners

insights.claim: The hosts' Porterhouse strategy had to trim Valero for the first time since inception because it breached the position-size limit, though Valero remains its largest holding.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: The managers still hold Valero as a high-conviction position.

insights.claim: Ideas like the refiners can only be found by screening the market's best-performing stocks; nobody would have predicted that a tiny XLE sub-industry would post AI-like returns. Not every screen winner keeps winning, so stop losses are needed.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A momentum or relative-strength screen with risk management catches outliers that top-down analysis misses.
insights.quote: You should be looking at the best stocks in the market.
